::: {.lead}
In a space station game, the airlock opens only when the player has the pass
and the suit has oxygen. An alarm rings when the oxygen is gone. A radio
works when exactly one of two antennas is on. Every one of these rules is a
sentence that is **true or false** at each moment, and the game checks it
many times per second. Mathematics calls such sentences **propositions**, and
joins them with **logical operators**: NOT, AND, OR, XOR and IF–THEN. In this
lesson you learn the value of each operator, build longer conditions with
brackets, and list every case of a rule in a **truth table**. Every section
ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary proposition truth-value boolean-variable logical-operator negation conjunction disjunction exclusive-or implication compound-proposition operator-precedence truth-table >}}

## 11.1 Propositions: true or false

A game asks itself questions all the time: Does the player have the key? Is
the health 0? Is the boss defeated? The answer is always yes or no
(@fig-prop).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 11.1 — Proposition"}
A **proposition** is a statement that is either **true** or **false**, not
both. Its **truth value** is T (true, 1) or F (false, 0). We name
propositions with small letters: p, q, r. In code, a proposition is a
**Boolean variable** (`bool`).
:::

![Propositions and sentences that are not propositions.](images/propositions.png){#fig-prop width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.1 — Propositions of a space station"}
1. p: "The player has the pass." In code: `bool hasPass`.
2. q: "The suit has oxygen." `bool hasOxygen`.
3. r: "The hull is broken." `hull == 0`, true or false.
4. "3 > 5" is a proposition too: it is false.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Calling "health > 50" a proposition while health is unknown. It becomes a
proposition (true or false) only when health has a value. Orders ("Open
the door!") and questions are never propositions.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Find the propositions"}
1. Write three propositions about a racing game (for example, "the car is
   on the track").
2. Write one sentence that is not a proposition, and say why.

*Your result:* four sentences.
::: {.check}
A good answer: "the car is on the track", "the lap is finished", "the
speed is over 100" (each true or false at every moment); "Drive faster!" is
not a proposition: it is an order, not true or false. Check: each
proposition can be answered with true or false; the last sentence is an
order, a question or an opinion.
:::
:::

## 11.2 NOT, AND, OR and XOR

Two propositions can be joined into a new one. The three basic operators
are NOT, AND and OR (@fig-nao).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 11.2 — NOT, AND, OR"}
- **Negation** ¬p (NOT p) is true when p is false.
- **Conjunction** p ∧ q (p AND q) is true only when **both** are true.
- **Disjunction** p ∨ q (p OR q) is true when **at least one** is true.

In C#: `!p`, `p && q`, `p || q`.
:::

![The value of NOT, AND and OR in each of the four cases.](images/not-and-or.png){#fig-nao width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.2 — Airlock, hatch and alarm"}
The player has the pass (p = T), but the suit has no oxygen (q = F).

1. Airlock, p ∧ q: T ∧ F = **F**. It stays shut.
2. Cargo hatch, p ∨ q: T ∨ F = **T**. It opens.
3. The alarm ¬q: ¬F = **T**. It rings.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/logic-lab.html" poster="sims/logic-lab.png" title="Logic Lab: NOT, AND, OR, XOR and IF–THEN" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that OR means "one but not both". In logic and in code, p ∨ q is
also true when both are true.
:::

### XOR: exactly one

A radio on the station works when exactly one of two antennas is on: not
none, not both. Everyday "or" sometimes means this; logic gives it its own
name (@fig-xi).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 11.3 — Exclusive or"}
**Exclusive or** p ⊕ q (p XOR q) is true when **exactly one** of p and q is
true. It is false when both are true and when both are false. In C# for
`bool` values: `p ^ q` (or `p != q`).
:::

![XOR and IF–THEN for the four cases.](images/xor-implies.png){#fig-xi width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.3 — The radio"}
1. Antenna A on, B off: T ⊕ F = **T**. The radio works.
2. Both on: T ⊕ T = **F**. They interfere, and the radio is silent.
3. A game of two players: "exactly one player holds the flag" is
   holdsA ⊕ holdsB.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Using OR for "either the sword or the shield, not both". `sword || shield`
also lets the player take both. Use XOR.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Four cases in Logic Lab"}
1. In **Logic Lab**, set p and q to each of the four cases. Write the values
   of ¬p, p ∧ q, p ∨ q and p ⊕ q for each case.
2. For each rule, choose OR or XOR: (a) "attack with a sword or a bow, one
   at a time"; (b) "the alarm rings when a door or a window opens".

*Your result:* a table of four rows and two answers.

::: {.check}
(T, T): F, T, T, F. (T, F): F, F, T, T. (F, T): T, F, T, T. (F, F): T, F, F, F
(¬p, p ∧ q, p ∨ q, p ⊕ q). (a) XOR: one at a time, not both. (b) OR: the alarm
also rings when both open.
:::
:::

## 11.3 IF–THEN: implication

The designer writes a rule: "If the reactor is off, then the lights are
red." When is this rule **broken**? Only when the reactor is off and the
lights are not red (@fig-xi).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 11.4 — Implication"}
The **implication** p → q (IF p THEN q) is false only when p is true and q
is false. In every other case it is true. It has the same value as
¬p ∨ q. In p → q, p is the **condition** and q the **result**.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.4 — Checking the reactor rule"}
p: "the reactor is off"; q: "the lights are red".

1. Reactor off, lights red: T → T = T. The rule is kept.
2. Reactor off, lights not red: T → F = **F**. A bug: the warning is
   missing.
3. Reactor on: F → T and F → F are both T. The rule says nothing about a
   running reactor.
4. A test in code: `if (reactorOff && !lightsRed) ReportBug();`
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Turning the rule round. "If the reactor is off, then the lights are red" is
not "if the lights are red, then the reactor is off": the lights may be red
for another reason, such as a fire.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · When is the rule broken?"}
Rule: "If the level is finished, then all coins are collected." Write the
one case that breaks it, and the C# condition that finds it.

*Your result:* one sentence and one condition.
::: {.check}
The rule is broken when the level is finished but not all coins are
collected: `levelFinished && !allCoins`.
:::
:::

## 11.4 Compound propositions and brackets

Real rules join several operators. The supply shop of the station sells
when it is open and the player has coins or a card. The order of
the operators decides the meaning (@fig-prec).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 11.5 — Compound propositions and precedence"}
A **compound proposition** joins propositions with several operators. The
**operator precedence** is: first **NOT**, then **AND**, then **OR**
(IF–THEN last). Brackets are computed first. So p ∧ q ∨ r means
(p ∧ q) ∨ r.
:::

![The same words with and without brackets.](images/precedence.png){#fig-prec width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.5 — The supply shop"}
Shop closed (s = F), no coins (c = F), a card (k = T).

1. s ∧ (c ∨ k) = F ∧ (F ∨ T) = F ∧ T = **F**: nothing is sold.
2. s ∧ c ∨ k = (F ∧ F) ∨ T = F ∨ T = **T**: the shop sells, a bug.
3. The rule needs the brackets.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Writing a long condition without brackets and trusting it. Write the
brackets whenever AND and OR meet; the next reader (and you, later) will
see the rule at once.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Compute"}
p = T, q = F, r = T. Compute (a) p ∨ q ∧ r; (b) (p ∨ q) ∧ r;
(c) ¬p ∨ ¬q.

*Your result:* three truth values.
::: {.check}
(a) q ∧ r first: F ∧ T = F; then T ∨ F = **T**. (b) (T ∨ F) ∧ T = **T**.
(c) ¬T ∨ ¬F = F ∨ T = **T**.
:::
:::

## 11.5 Every case at once: truth tables

A game rule with two conditions has four possible situations: both true,
only the first, only the second, none. A truth table writes all of them
down, in a fixed order (@fig-rows).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 11.6 — Truth table"}
A **truth table** has one column for each variable and one row for each
combination of truth values. With **n** variables there are $2^n$ rows: 2
variables give 4 rows, 3 give 8, 4 give 16. The usual order: in the first
column half the rows are T, half F; in each next column T and F change
twice as often.
:::

![Truth tables with 2 and 3 variables.](images/tt-rows.png){#fig-rows width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.6 — Two conditions of a door"}
p: "the ship has the pass", q: "the shields are up".

1. 2 variables: $2^2 = 4$ rows.
2. Rows: (T, T), (T, F), (F, T), (F, F).
3. With a third variable r ("an officer is on board"), each row splits in
   two: $2^3 = 8$ rows.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Writing the rows in a random order. It is easy to miss a case or write one
twice. Follow the halving pattern, and count: 2, 4, 8 or 16 rows.
:::

### A compound proposition, column by column

For a longer proposition, add one column for each part, from the inside out
(@fig-steps). The last column is the value of the whole proposition.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 11.7 — Helper columns"}
To build the truth table of a compound proposition, add a **helper
column** for each operator, in the order of computing (brackets, NOT, AND,
OR, IF–THEN). Each helper column uses only the columns before it.
:::

![¬(p ∧ ¬q), one column at a time.](images/tt-steps.png){#fig-steps width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.7 — The table of ¬(p ∧ ¬q)"}
1. Column ¬q: F, T, F, T.
2. Column p ∧ ¬q: only the row p = T, q = F gives T.
3. Column ¬(p ∧ ¬q): T, F, T, T. It is false only when p = T and q = F —
   the same as p → q.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/truth-table-lab.html" poster="sims/truth-table-lab.png" title="Truth Table Lab: every case of a condition" height="700" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Computing the NOT of a whole bracket as the NOT of each part: ¬(p ∧ q) is
not ¬p ∧ ¬q. Compute the bracket first, then turn the whole column round
(Lecture 12 gives the right law).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Predict, then check"}
1. On paper, build the table of (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬p with helper columns.
2. In **Truth Table Lab**, switch to Quiz mode, type the same condition and
   enter your answers. Press Check.

*Your result:* a table and your check.
::: {.check}
Columns p ∨ q, ¬p and (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬p for the rows (T, T), (T, F), (F, T),
(F, F): T, F, F; T, F, F; T, T, **T**; F, T, F. It is true only when p = F and
q = T. Truth Table Lab marks all four answers right.
:::
:::

## 11.6 A game rule as a truth table

A truth table shows a designer exactly when a rule fires. Here is the dock
door of a space game with three conditions (@fig-door).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 11.8 — Reading a rule from its table"}
The **true rows** of a rule are the situations in which it fires (the door
opens, the trap triggers). Reading them answers two questions: does it fire
in every case it should, and in no case it should not?
:::

![The dock door p ∧ (q ∨ r): it opens in 3 of 8 cases.](images/door-table.png){#fig-door width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.8 — Checking the dock door"}
p: pass, q: shields up, r: officer on board. Rule: p ∧ (q ∨ r).

1. True rows: (T, T, T), (T, T, F), (T, F, T): 3 of 8.
2. Without the pass the door never opens: rows 5–8 are all F. Good.
3. With the pass but neither shields nor officer, it stays shut: row 4. The
   designer agrees: no bug.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Checking only the "normal" case (everything true). Bugs hide in unusual
rows, such as the pass without shields.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The repair bay"}
The repair bay opens when the ship is docked (d) and the engine is off (¬e),
or when an officer is on board (o): (d ∧ ¬e) ∨ o. Build its 8-row table. In
how many cases does it open?

*Your result:* a table and a number.
::: {.check}
It opens in the rows (T, F, T), (T, F, F), (T, T, T), (F, T, T) and (F, F, T)
of (d, e, o): **5 of 8** cases. With an officer on board it always opens;
without one, only when the ship is docked and the engine is off.
:::
:::

## Case study: Door Logic

*Torch Hall* is a made-up dungeon game. Its designer writes every door rule
in words: the iron door needs the key and a torch; the wooden door needs
the key or a torch; a trap fires without a torch; a lever works when exactly
one switch is up; the crown rule "if crown, then boss defeated" must be
checked; and the last gate needs the defeated boss and the key or a torch.
The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses these rules. In the
mini-game below you choose the condition for each door.

{{< sim file="sims/door-logic.html" poster="sims/door-logic.png" title="Door Logic: the condition for each door" kind="game" height="640" >}}

## Further reading

Rosen, *Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications*, 8th ed., Sections 1.1
and 1.2 (propositional logic and its applications). Microsoft Learn,
"Boolean logical operators (C# reference)".

## Exercises

1. Is "Collect all the coins!" a proposition? Why?
2. p = T, q = F. Find ¬p, p ∧ q and p ∨ q.
3. When is p ∨ q false?
4. p = T, q = T. Find p ⊕ q.
5. p = F, q = F. Find p → q.
6. Which case breaks the rule p → q?
7. In which order are NOT, AND and OR computed?
8. p = F, q = T, r = T. Find p ∧ q ∨ r and p ∧ (q ∨ r).
9. Write in C#: "the shop is open when it is day and the player is not in a
   fight".
10. How many rows has the truth table of 4 variables?
11. Build the truth table of p ∧ ¬q.
12. The rule p ∨ (q ∧ r). In how many of the 8 cases is it true?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. No: it is an order, not a statement that is true or false.
2. ¬p = F; p ∧ q = F; p ∨ q = T.
3. Only when both p and q are false.
4. F.
5. T.
6. p true and q false.
7. NOT first, then AND, then OR.
8. (F ∧ T) ∨ T = T; F ∧ (T ∨ T) = F.
9. `isDay && !inFight`.
10. $2^4 = 16$.
11. T only in the row p = T, q = F: F, T, F, F.
12. 5: the 4 rows with p = T, and (F, T, T).
:::
